vignette: He sits across from me, shoulders rounded as if bracing for a blow that isn't coming. At thirty-five, his face carries a stillness that belongs to someone decades older. The first time he spoke about the basement, his voice barely rises above the hum of the ceiling fan. Three years ago, in a cramped concrete holding cell in a Southeastern province, he is bound to a metal chair for eleven days. The interrogators are never interested in information; they are interested in breaking the rhythm of his breath. He remembers the cold floor against his bare feet, the metallic taste of dried blood, the way the guard's boots echo like a metronome counting down to the next injury. He does not describe the acts in graphic detail. He describes the silence that follows, the way his mind retreats into a narrow corridor where time stops and sound turns to static. He escapes during a sudden power outage, stumbles through monsoon rain until his hands find the phone number of an aid organization. He arrives in this city six months later, divorce papers signed in a language that still tastes like ash. He works as an accountant now, or tries to. His desk is pristine, every pen aligned, every spreadsheet color-coded to a fault. Precision is his armor. But the numbers no longer behave like they used to. When he sits at his computer, the cursor blinks like a warning light. He checks the same cell seventeen times, convinced that a misplaced decimal will summon the basement back into his apartment. His supervisor notices the delayed reports, the empty chair during mandatory team lunches. He avoids the fluorescent lights, the smell of damp concrete, the sound of heavy footsteps in the hallway. When his phone buzzes, his heart drops to his stomach. He stares at the screen until it goes dark, pretending he never saw it. Sleep has become a foreign country. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. every night, not from a dream, but from the sudden awareness that he is breathing. His chest tightens, his palms sweat, and he sits on the edge of the bed until his pulse syncs with the traffic outside. He drinks black coffee by noon and watches the street through two layers of curtains. His former partner left after the first year back, unable to navigate the walls he had learned to build overnight. He does not blame her. He understands, in a detached way, that intimacy requires a nervous system at rest, and his is always sounding alarms. Friends send group messages he never replies to. He scrolls through their vacation photos with a hollow ache, remembering laughter as something that happened to other people. On Tuesdays at 4 p.m., he comes to this office and places his wallet on the table with the same careful deliberation he uses to reconcile accounts. He watches the dust motes dance in the afternoon light and waits for permission to speak. When he does, his words are measured, stripped of excess, as if vocabulary itself could be weaponized. He describes the weight of carrying a body that remembers what the mind has tried to bury. He notes how tax season makes his fingers twitch, how the sound of a stapler feels like a gunshot, how he now walks the perimeter of every room he enters. He does not ask for relief. He asks, sometimes, how to trust his own hands again. I listen as he maps the architecture of his survival, noting the careful distance he keeps between himself and the present moment, the quiet erosion of a man who learned that safety is an illusion he can no longer afford to imagine.
